newsitem.title: UK: Studies find more evidence that marijuana may hook.
newsitem.headline: Studies find more evidence that marijuana may hook.

text.p: Two teams of scientists said on Friday they had found strong evidence that marijuana can act as a "gateway" drug helping users get hooked on the harder stuff.
One study shows marijuana, or cannabis, activates the same part of the brain that heroin and cocaine do, while the second shows that rats go through withdrawal from cannabis.
They indicated that marijuana can change brain chemistry and that the grumpiness some users report when they stop taking it could be true withdrawal symptoms.

"These two studies supply important evidence that marijuana acts on the same neural substrates and has the same effects as drugs already known to be highly addictive," David Friedman, a neurobiologist at the Bowman Gray School of Medicine in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, told the journal Science.

Fernando Rodriguez de Fonseca and colleagues at Universidad Complutense de Madrid looked at corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF), which other research indicates plays a role in symptoms caused by withdrawal from alcohol, cocaine and heroin.

They gave potent marijuana extracts to rats for two weeks to simulate the effects of long-term use. They then used a drug to create rapid clearing of the cannabis from the rats' systems. Cannabis usually leaves the body slowly.
Reporting in Science, they said the rats showed "marked elevation" of CRF levels and other brain changes. They also acted anxious.
"These changes are consistent with the irritability and discomfort that have been described to occur after cessation of long-term consumption of marijuana," they wrote.
This could "prime" the brain, making a user more receptive to "harder" drugs, they added.
"The work suggests that the CRF system may be a part of a common experience in withdrawal -- that is, anxiety," Alan Leshner, director of the U.S. National Institute on Drug Abuse, told Science.
A second study looked at the effect of cannabis on dopamine, an important neurotransmitter or message-carrying chemical.

Some research indicates that drugs can 'hijack' the body's reward system, which is supposed to motivate people and other animals to seek food, sex and other basic needs. Surges of dopamine are key to this reward system.
Gaetano Di Chiari and colleagues at the University of Rome found that THC, the active ingredient in cannabis, caused dopamine levels to skyrocket in rats.
The effect was similar to that of heroin, they said.
They also found that naloxene, a drug known to block the effect of heroin, also blocked the effects of THC in the rats.
"Although our results do not provide direct evidence for a causal relation between cannabis and heroin use, they are nonetheless consistent with this possibility," they concluded.
"I would be satisfied if, following all this evidence, people would no longer consider THC (the active ingredient of cannabis) a 'soft' drug," Di Chiari told Science.
